title: US aid runs dry as new fighting razes Yemen
gist: Yemen is sliding back into full-scale war after a Houthi offensive seized Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while US and international aid cuts have hollowed out relief; Taiz is encircled and cholera is tripling.

insights.claim: Last month the Houthis launched a lightning offensive, captured large areas of Red Sea coastal territory from the Saudi-backed government and gained control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hagedorn
insights.so_what: Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb raises Red Sea shipping, insurance and energy-route risk.

insights.claim: Yemen is returning to full-scale war with a humanitarian system hollowed out by international funding cuts, including nearly all aid from the United States, once its largest donor.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hagedorn
insights.so_what: Aid retrenchment amplifies the humanitarian impact of renewed fighting and may increase displacement and instability.

insights.claim: The Houthi encirclement of Taiz has driven food prices up 50% since early September and caused severe fuel shortages, and the World Food Programme says it lost access to more than 600,000 trapped people.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hagedorn
insights.so_what: Siege dynamics point to worsening famine risk and possible mass displacement.

insights.claim: Yemen's foreign minister called the siege of Taiz a 'war crime' meant to wear down residents' resistance, while the Houthis have urged government forces in the city to surrender.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hagedorn
insights.so_what: Signals a possible coercive endgame in Taiz.

insights.claim: More than 213,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the fighting, and WHO says suspected cholera cases tripled in three weeks owing to camp overcrowding and unsafe water.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hagedorn
insights.so_what: Disease outbreak and displacement raise the odds of larger spillover refugee and aid-demand shocks.
